quotes.t: Hatred paralyzes life; love releases it. Hatred confuses life; love harmonizes it. Hatred darkens life; love illuminates it.
Cowardice asks the question, 'Is it safe?' Expediency asks the question, 'Is it politic?' Vanity asks the question, 'Is it popular?' But conscience asks the question, 'Is it right?'.
quotes.source: Remaining Awake Through a Great Revolution, 31 March 1968

quotes.t: There comes a time when silence is betrayal.
quotes.source: A Time to Break Silence, Riverside Church, 4 April 1967

quotes.t: Men often hate each other because they fear each other; they fear each other because they don't know each other; they don't know each other because they can not communicate; they can not communicate because they are separated.
I can listen no longer in silence. I must speak to you by such means as are within my reach.
I could not be happy with a man whose taste did not in every point coincide with my own.
Men have had every advantage of us in telling their own story. Education has been theirs in so much higher a degree; the pen has been in their hands. I will not allow books to prove anything.
All the privilege I claim for my own sex (it is not a very enviable one; you need not covet it), is that of loving longest, when existence or when hope is gone.

I sit on a man's back, choking him and making him carry me, and yet assure myself and others that I am very sorry for him and wish to ease his lot by all possible means — except by getting off his back.
quotes.source: What Then Must We Do?, ch. 16 (1886)

quotes.t: Maybe I did not live as I ought to have done.
quotes.source: The Death of Ivan Ilyich, ch. 9 (1886)

quotes.t: Yes, love, but not the love that loves for something, to gain something, or because of something, but that love that I felt for the first time, when dying, I saw my enemy and yet loved him.

Pierre was right when he said that one must believe in the possibility of happiness in order to be happy, and I now believe in it. Let the dead bury the dead, but while I'm alive, I must live and be happy.
Deep down, the young are lonelier than the old.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl, 8 July 1944

quotes.t: How noble and good everyone could be if, at the end of each day, they were to review their own behavior and weigh up the rights and wrongs. They would automatically try to do better at the start of each new day and, after a while, would certainly accomplish a great deal.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl, 6 July 1944

quotes.t: I must work, so as not to be a fool, to get on, to become a journalist, because that's what I want!
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl, 5 April 1944

quotes.t: Exclusion is never the way forward on our shared paths to freedom and justice.
The quality of human life on our planet is nothing more than the sum total of our daily interactions with one another.
I would like to share with you two simple truths: there is nothing that cannot be forgiven, and there is no one un-deserving of forgiveness.
It is the function of art to renew our perception. What we are familiar with we cease to see.
quotes.source: The Novel of the Future (1968), ch. 2

quotes.t: There are two ways to reach me: by way of kisses or by way of the imagination. But there is a hierarchy: the kisses alone don't work.
There are many ways to be free. One of them is to transcend reality by imagination, as I try to do.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. IV (June 1945)

quotes.t: To forget the wrongs you receive, is to remedy them.
He invites crime who ignores sin.
quotes.source: Sententiae (Latin: Invitat culpam qui peccatum praeterit)

quotes.t: No tears are shed, when an enemy dies.
The man without a purpose is like a ship without a rudder.
A loving heart is the beginning of all knowledge.
No sadder proof can be given by a man of his own littleness than disbelief in great men.
The older one grows, the more one likes indecency.
quotes.source: The String Quartet, Monday or Tuesday (1921)

quotes.t: It's not catastrophes, murders, deaths, diseases, that age and kill us; it's the way people look and laugh, and run up the steps of omnibuses.
Blame it or praise it, there is no denying the wild horse in us.
Solitude was my only consolation — deep, dark, deathlike solitude.
I beheld the corruption of death succeed to the blooming cheek of life; I saw how the worm inherited the wonders of the eye and brain.
We are unfashioned creatures, but half made up, if one wiser, better, dearer than ourselves — such a friend ought to be — do not lend his aid to perfectionate our weak and faulty natures.
When I have fears that I may cease to be before my pen has glean'd my teeming brain
quotes.source: When I Have Fears That I May Cease to Be (sonnet, 1818)

quotes.t: Then felt I like some watcher of the skies when a new planet swims into his ken
quotes.source: On First Looking into Chapman's Homer (sonnet, 1816)

quotes.t: I have loved the principle of beauty in all things, and if I had had time I would have made myself remembered.
No one wants to die. Even people who want to go to heaven don't want to die to get there.
Don't be trapped by dogma — which is living with the results of other people's thinking.
Remembering that you are going to die is the best way I know to avoid the trap of thinking you have something to lose.
On the 26th of January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions. In politics we will have equality and in social and economic life we will have inequality.
quotes.source: Speech to the Constituent Assembly (25 November 1949)

quotes.t: I solemnly assure you that I will not die a Hindu.
quotes.source: Speech at the Depressed Classes Conference, Yeola (13 October 1935)

quotes.t: Caste does not result in economic efficiency. Caste cannot improve, and has not improved, race. Caste has, however, done one thing. It has completely disorganised and demoralised the Hindus.
To understand yourself is the beginning of wisdom.
When you call yourself an Indian or a Muslim or a Christian or a European, or anything else, you are being violent.
Meditation is not a means to an end. It is both the means and the end.

It is not book-learning young men need, nor instruction about this and that, but a stiffening of the vertebrae which will cause them to be loyal to a trust, to act promptly, concentrate their energies: do the thing — 'Carry a message to Garcia.'
Art is not a thing; it is a way.
quotes.source: The Note Book of Elbert Hubbard (1927)

quotes.t: Every man is a damn fool for at least five minutes every day; wisdom consists in not exceeding the limit.
quotes.source: The Note Book of Elbert Hubbard (1927)

quotes.t: Walking is the best possible exercise. Habituate yourself to walk very far.
Experience hath shewn, that even under the best forms of government those entrusted with power have, in time, and by slow operations, perverted it into tyranny.
quotes.source: A Bill for the More General Diffusion of Knowledge (1778)

quotes.t: A little patience, and we shall see the reign of witches pass over, their spells dissolve, and the people, recovering their true sight, restore their government to its true principles.

What can you do if you are thirty and, turning the corner of your own street, you are overcome, suddenly, by a feeling of bliss — absolute bliss! — as though you'd suddenly swallowed a bright piece of that late afternoon sun and it burned in your bosom, sending out a little shower of sparks into every particle, into every finger and toe?
Whenever I prepare for a journey I prepare as though for death. Should I never return, all is in order. This is what life has taught me.
quotes.source: Journal entry (29 January 1922), The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927)

quotes.t: Oh, how fascinating it was! How she enjoyed it! How she loved sitting here, watching it all!
quotes.source: Miss Brill (1920), The Garden Party and Other Stories

quotes.t: There is a certain pleasure in weeping.
quotes.source: Tristia, Book 4, poem 3 (Est quaedam flere voluptas)

quotes.t: Majesty and love go ill together.
So long as you are secure you will count many friends; if your life becomes clouded you will be alone.
quotes.source: Tristia, Book 1, poem 9 (trans. Arthur Leslie Wheeler)

quotes.t: Happiness quite unshared can scarcely be called happiness; it has no taste.
quotes.source: Letter, quoted in Elizabeth Gaskell, The Life of Charlotte Brontë (1857), Vol. 2, ch. 5

quotes.t: I can live alone, if self-respect, and circumstances require me so to do. I need not sell my soul to buy bliss.
Feeling without judgment is a washy draught indeed; but judgment untempered by feeling is too bitter and husky a morsel for human deglutition.
The life of the nation is secure only while the nation is honest, truthful, and virtuous.
quotes.source: Speech on the 23rd anniversary of Emancipation in the District of Columbia, April 1885

quotes.t: To me, every hour of the light and dark is a miracle.
It is the peculiar quality of a fool to perceive the faults of others, and to forget his own.
I don't wait for moods. You accomplish nothing if you do that. Your mind must know it has got to get down to work.
Life is now. There was never a time when your life was not now, nor will there ever be.
Brevity is the sister of talent.
quotes.source: Letter to Alexander P. Chekhov, 11 April 1889

quotes.t: Just as a diamond can only be polished by another diamond, it is only through genuine, all-out engagement with others that people can polish their character, and help each other to reach greater heights.
To be a great champion you must believe you are the best. If you're not, pretend you are.
quotes.source: Muhammad Ali Center, "In His Own Words"

quotes.t: If you go looking for a friend, you're going to find they're very scarce. If you go out to be a friend, you'll find them everywhere.
quotes.source: As quoted in The Power of Respect (2009)

quotes.t: Though much is taken, much abides; and though we are not now that strength which in old days moved earth and heaven, that which we are, we are.
Everything comes to him who hustles while he waits.
quotes.source: As quoted in Thomas Alva Edison: Sixty Years of an Inventor's Life (1908), p. 14

quotes.t: Work harder on yourself than you do on your job.
quotes.source: Jim Rohn (from his mentor Earl Shoaff)

quotes.t: You cannot hope to build a better world without improving the individuals.
In the business world, the rearview mirror is always clearer than the windshield.

I decided, very early on, just to accept life unconditionally; I never expected it to do anything special for me, yet I seemed to accomplish far more than I had ever hoped. Most of the time it just happened to me without my ever seeking it.
quotes.source: Audrey Hepburn: A Life in Pictures (2007)

quotes.t: I remain just one thing, and one thing only — and that is a clown. It places me on a far higher plane than any politician.
quotes.source: As quoted in The Observer, 17 June 1960

quotes.t: When dealing with people, remember you are not dealing with creatures of logic, but with creatures bristling with prejudice and motivated by pride and vanity.
quotes.source: How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936)

quotes.t: Hope is a good breakfast, but it is a bad supper.
Curiosity is one of the permanent and certain characteristics of a vigorous intellect.
In the end, you're measured not by how much you undertake but by what you finally accomplish.
quotes.source: Trump: The Art of the Deal (1987), p. 355

quotes.t: For after all, the best thing one can do when it is raining, is to let it rain.
quotes.source: Tales of a Wayside Inn, "The Poet's Tale" (1863)

quotes.t: An honest man's the noblest work of God.
quotes.source: An Essay on Man, Epistle IV, line 247 (1733-34)

quotes.t: The great end of all human industry is the attainment of happiness.
quotes.source: "The Stoic", Essays, Moral, Political, and Literary, Part I, Essay XVI

quotes.t: When we love, we always strive to become better than we are. When we strive to become better than we are, everything around us becomes better too.
We do not need magic to change the world, we carry all the power we need inside ourselves already: we have the power to imagine better.

When you meet the one among the millions, when amid millions of years, across the borderless wastes of time, you happen to catch him or her, neither a step too early nor a step too late, what else is there to do except to ask softly: "So you're here, too?"
He said not 'Thou shalt not be tempested, thou shalt not be travailed, thou shalt not be dis-eased'; but he said, 'Thou shalt not be overcome.'
It is perfectly true, as the philosophers say, that life must be understood backwards. But they forget the other proposition, that it must be lived forwards.
Order and simplification are the first steps toward the mastery of a subject — the actual enemy is the unknown.
Bulla, what do I know of who I am?
The only difference between me and a madman is that I'm not mad.
quotes.source: Remarks during a 1934 visit to Hartford, Connecticut, reported in contemporary newspapers

quotes.t: Do not be afraid. Open wide the doors for Christ.
quotes.source: Homily for the Inauguration of his Pontificate, 22 October 1978

quotes.t: A novel is a mirror carried along a high road.
Who says my poems are poems? My poems are not poems. When you know that my poems are not poems, then we can speak of poetry.
I'm for truth, no matter who tells it. I'm for justice, no matter who it is for or against.
Mystery creates wonder and wonder is the basis of man's desire to understand.
quotes.source: Address to a Joint Session of Congress, 16 September 1969

quotes.t: The power to question is the basis of all human progress.
Hope lies in dreams, in imagination, and in the courage of those who dare to make dreams into reality.
quotes.source: Address on receiving the Nehru Award, 10 January 1977

quotes.t: The good we secure for ourselves is precarious and uncertain, is floating in mid-air, until it is secured for all of us and incorporated into our common life.
Time is the coin of your life. It is the only coin you have, and only you can determine how it will be spent. Be careful lest you let other people spend it for you.
quotes.source: Speech at his 85th birthday dinner, 6 January 1963

Alexander Pope.bio: English poet and master of the heroic couplet. His works include An Essay on Criticism, The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Man, along with celebrated translations of Homer.

Alfred Tennyson.bio: English Poet Laureate; author of In Memoriam and Ulysses.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Audrey Hepburn.bio: Audrey Hepburn was a British actress and humanitarian celebrated for films such as Roman Holiday, Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady. In later life she devoted herself to UNICEF, serving as a Goodwill Ambassador in some of the world's poorest regions.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Bulleh Shah.bio: Punjabi Sufi poet and humanist. His kafis challenge religious ritualism and caste, and are still widely sung today.

Carl Sandburg.bio: American poet, journalist and historian. He won three Pulitzer Prizes, two for poetry collections such as Chicago Poems and one for his biography of Abraham Lincoln.

Charlie Chaplin.bio: Charlie Chaplin was an English comic actor and filmmaker whose Little Tramp became a global icon of silent cinema. He co-founded United Artists and wrote, directed and starred in classics including City Lights, Modern Times and The Great Dictator.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Dale Carnegie.bio: Dale Carnegie was an American writer and lecturer on self-improvement and public speaking. His book How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936) became one of the best-selling books of all time.

David Hume.bio: David Hume was a Scottish Enlightenment philosopher, historian and economist, best known for A Treatise of Human Nature and An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding. His scepticism about causation, miracles and the self profoundly influenced Western philosophy.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Donald Trump.bio: Donald Trump is an American businessman and television personality who served as the 45th President of the United States (2017–2021) and was elected again as the 47th President in 2024. Before politics he built a real-estate business and hosted the reality show The Apprentice.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Eileen Chang.bio: Eileen Chang was a Chinese writer celebrated for her psychologically sharp fiction of love and war in 1940s Shanghai and Hong Kong, including Lust, Caution and Love in a Fallen City. She later lived in the United States.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Francis Bacon.bio: Francis Bacon was an English philosopher, statesman and essayist who championed the empirical method of inquiry. His Essays and his plan for the reform of learning in the Novum Organum helped lay the groundwork of modern science.

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow.bio: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow was an American poet and educator, among the most popular poets of his century. He wrote Paul Revere's Ride, The Song of Hiawatha and Evangeline, and produced the first American translation of Dante's Divine Comedy.

Indira Gandhi.bio: Indira Gandhi was the first and only woman prime minister of India, serving 1966–1977 and again from 1980 until her assassination in 1984. The daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, she led India through war, the Green Revolution and the controversial Emergency.

J.K. Rowling.bio: British author (1965– ), creator of Harry Potter.

Jane Addams.bio: Jane Addams was an American settlement activist and reformer who co-founded Hull House in Chicago, a model for community social work. She became the first American woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, in 1931.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

Jim Rohn.bio: Emanuel James Rohn, known as Jim Rohn, was an American entrepreneur and motivational speaker whose seminars and books on personal development influenced a generation of speakers, including Tony Robbins.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

John Paul II.bio: John Paul II, born Karol Wojtyła in Poland, was pope of the Roman Catholic Church from 1978 to 2005, one of the longest pontificates in history. A former actor and philosopher, his travels, writings and role in the fall of European communism made him a global moral figure.

Jonas Salk.bio: Jonas Salk was an American physician and virologist who developed one of the first successful polio vaccines, announced in 1955. He later founded the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in California.

Julian of Norwich.bio: Julian of Norwich was an English anchoress who lived in a cell attached to a church in Norwich and wrote the earliest surviving book in English by a woman. Her Revelations of Divine Love, recording visions she received during a grave illness, is famed for its message of hope.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Malcolm X.bio: Malcolm X (1925–1965) was an American human rights activist and leading voice of the civil rights era, known for his powerful speeches on Black dignity and self-determination.

Marie Curie.bio: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who pioneered the study of radioactivity, a term she coined. She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911 — and died of illness caused by her long exposure to radiation.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

Neil Armstrong.bio: American astronaut and the first person to walk on the Moon, during Apollo 11 in 1969.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Paulo Coelho.bio: Brazilian lyricist and novelist whose novel The Alchemist became one of the best-selling books in history, translated into dozens of languages. His fables about following one's dreams have inspired readers on every continent.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Ryokan.bio: Ryokan was a Japanese Zen monk who lived as a hermit in a small hut, writing gentle poems and playing with village children. Offered charity all his life, he owned almost nothing and is remembered for his warmth and simplicity.

Salvador Dalí.bio: Salvador Dalí was a Spanish Surrealist artist famous for dreamlike images such as the melting clocks of The Persistence of Memory. A brilliant self-publicist and technician, he worked in painting, film, sculpture and design from his base in Catalonia.

Samuel Johnson.bio: Samuel Johnson was an English writer who compiled the first great Dictionary of the English Language in 1755. Poet, essayist and the most quoted conversationalist of his age, his life was immortalised in Boswell's famous biography.

Soren Kierkegaard.bio: Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish philosopher, theologian and poet widely regarded as the first existentialist thinker. His works, including Fear and Trembling and Either/Or, explored faith, anxiety, despair and the individual's subjective relationship to truth.

Stendhal.bio: Stendhal, the pen name of Marie-Henri Beyle, was a French novelist whose The Red and the Black and The Charterhouse of Parma pioneered psychological realism. Little appreciated in his lifetime, he predicted his fame would begin around 1880 — and was right.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Edison.bio: Thomas Edison was an American inventor who developed the phonograph, the motion picture camera and the first practical electric light bulb. He held over a thousand US patents and founded the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Thomas Mann.bio: Thomas Mann was a German novelist whose Buddenbrooks, The Magic Mountain and Death in Venice dissect European bourgeois culture with irony and depth. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929 and spent the Nazi years in exile, broadcasting against Hitler from America.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Warren Buffett.bio: Investor Warren Buffett, the 'Oracle of Omaha', turned Berkshire Hathaway into one of the world's largest conglomerates through patient, disciplined value investing. Famous for his annual shareholder letters and frugal personal habits, he has pledged to give away the great majority of his fortune.

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
